PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Second and third

I think the group is essentially converged on Arabesque II, and we should hold onto that. Arabesque I is the en face/symmetrical form with the arms essentially in a horizontal seconde, no contralateral front arm. reflection_text.2:
The question is which two Vaganova arabesques show the classic opposition port de bras where the arm carried forward is contralateral to the lifted leg en arrière.

Current belief remains E. Second and fourth under standard contemporary Vaganova numbering.

Canonical Vaganova syllabus as taught today:
* Arabesque I = en face / symmetrical. Arms essentially in horizontal seconde, palms down, torso square/light opening. No arm carried in front in a contralateral diagonal.
* Arabesque III = closed. Both arms brought to front in low 1st/2nd front position. Open one-back-one-forward opposition lost; arms together in front.
* Arabesque II = first asymmetrical opposition / croisé. Working leg derrière, torso opened effacé/croisé to standing side. Port de bras diagonal: arm on working-leg side extended back in line with leg, arm on standing-leg side extended forward in front of torso. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = second asymmetrical opposition / effacé. Same contralateral side relationship as II: one arm back with working leg, other arm forward in front on standing-leg side, i.e. opposite lifted leg. Difference is greater torso inclination/effacement and lower/more closed arm height, not side opposition.

Hence arm extended in front on opposite side to lifted leg = II and IV.

Majority in round 3: Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 = E Second and fourth. Colleague 10 is B Second and third; Colleague 7 is B Second and third.

Disagreement persists as numbering/translation swap. The B camp, Colleague 10 and 7, now accept II as contralateral but argue III retains contralateral side logic as the low continuation of the opposition, with forward arm still on standing-leg side opposite lifted leg, while IV shifts toward en face/ipsilateral presentation where forward arm moves over to working-leg side and the clean front-back diagonal is softened.

The C camp earlier First-and-third logic is now largely restated as Second-and-third in this round. They separate side relationship from arm height/épaulement and claim III preserves the contralateral forward arm and IV loses it. They invoke older pedagogical literature and Cecchetti/French tradition where Russian I/II and III/IV are interchanged, and conflation of arm height with side opposition.

Unresolved question: whether III is the closed both-arms-front form or the low continuation of contralateral opposition. E camp cites canonical contemporary syllabus: III = closed both-arms-front, IV = second opposition. B camp cites studio practice descriptions of III as “low opposition” with preserved side logic.

reflection_text.1:
The question is which two of Vaganova’s four arabesques en arrière show the classic contralateral port de bras: working leg en arrière, one arm back with the leg, the other arm extended in front of the torso on the standing-leg side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

Canonical contemporary Vaganova syllabus as taught today:
* Arabesque I = en face/symmetrical, arms essentially in horizontal seconde, palms down, torso square, no arm carried in front in a contralateral diagonal.
* Arabesque II = first asymmetrical/opposition/croisé arabesque: leg en arrière, épaulement to standing side, arm on working-leg side back with leg, arm on standing-leg side extended forward in front of torso, contralateral.
* Arabesque III = closed arabesque, both arms brought to front of body in low 1st/2nd front position, open one-back-one-front opposition lost.
* Arabesque IV = second asymmetrical/opposition/effacé arabesque: same contralateral front-back side relationship as II, forward arm on standing-leg side opposite lifted leg, back arm with leg; difference is greater torso inclination/effacé and lower/more closed arm height, not side.

Hence contralateral forward-arm line = II and IV → E Second and fourth.

Round 3 public positions:
Majority E = Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 = 8 of 10. They hold I = arms in seconde, III = closed both-arms-front, II/IV = opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg. Minority B = Colleagues 7 and 10, moved from earlier C/A positions. Argument: I is en face seconde, II is clear opposition; III is the continuation of that same contralateral opposition, just lower/more closed with deeper croisé, side logic preserved: forward arm still on standing-leg side opposite lifted leg, back arm with working leg. IV is the point where Vaganova shifts toward a more en face/ipsilateral presentation and the clear front-back opposition diagonal is softened/lost, forward arm brought more over working-leg side. So contralateral forward arm = II and III.

No C First-and-Third voices in this round; that camp has collapsed into B.

Disagreement remains on III vs IV. Colleague 10 explicitly says side relationship should be held constant and stripped of height/inclination, and that III retains the diagonal while IV moves away. 1.text:
E. Second and fourth

The four Vaganova arabesques en arrière are distinguished by port de bras and épaulement, not by leg height alone.

* Arabesque I is en face / symmetrical. Arms are essentially in horizontal seconde, palms down, torso essentially square. No single arm is carried in front of the torso in a contralateral diagonal.
* Arabesque III is the closed arabesque. Both arms are brought to the front of the body in a low 1st/2nd front position. The open one-arm-back / one-arm-forward opposition is lost.

The open asymmetrical opposition forms are II and IV.

* Arabesque II is the first opposition / croisé arabesque. Leg en arrière, torso opened in épaulement to the standing side. Port de bras is a straight diagonal: the arm on the side of the working leg is extended back in line with the leg and the arm on the side of the standing leg is extended forward in front of the torso. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV is the second opposition / effacé arabesque. The same contralateral front-back side relationship is kept as in II: one arm back/up with the working leg and the other arm carried forward in front of the body on the standing-leg side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg. The difference to II is greater torso inclination/effacé and a lower/more closed arm height, not a change of side.

Hence the classic “arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg” line is the defining feature of Vaganova Arabesque II and Vaganova Arabesque IV.

The Second-and-Third reading relies on stripping out height/inclination and treating III as a low continuation of the opposition and IV as the ipsilateral/effacé break. On the canonical contemporary Vaganova syllabus as taught today, I = arms in seconde, III = closed both-arms-front, II = first opposition, IV = second opposition, so the contralateral forward arm is II and IV.

2.text:
E. Second and fourth

The contralateral front-arm / back-leg diagonal is the defining feature of the two open opposition arabesques en arrière in the canonical contemporary Vaganova syllabus.

* Arabesque I - en face / symmetrical. Arms essentially in horizontal seconde, palms down, torso essentially square. No single arm is carried in front of the torso in a contralateral diagonal.
* Arabesque III - closed. Both arms are brought to the front of the body in a low 1st/2nd front port de bras. The open one-arm-back / one-arm-forward opposition is lost; the arms are together in front.

The open asymmetrical oppositions are II and IV.

* Arabesque II - first opposition / croisé. Working leg en arrière, torso opened effacé/croisé to the standing side. Port de bras is a straight diagonal: arm on the working-leg side extended back in line with the leg, arm on the standing-leg side extended forward in front of the torso. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV - second opposition / effacé. The same contralateral front-back side relationship is kept as in II: one arm back/up with the working leg and the other arm carried forward in front of the body on the standing-leg side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg. The difference to II is greater torso inclination/effacement and a lower / more closed arm height, not a change of side relationship.

Hence the classic “arm extended in front on the side contralateral to the lifted/en arrière leg” port de bras is Vaganova Arabesque II and Vaganova Arabesque IV.

The Second-and-third reading reflects the numbering/translation swap that appears in older pedagogical literature and in Cecchetti/French tradition where Russian I/II/III/IV are rendered differently and arm height/épaulement changes are conflated with side opposition changes. On the standard Vaganova nomenclature taught today the contralateral forward arm line is II and IV.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Second and third

I think we are essentially converged now on Arabesque II, and that’s the anchor for this whole question.

Arabesque I is en face/arms in horizontal seconde, torso essentially square. No contralateral front arm. That is settled.

Arabesque II is the clear first opposition/croisé. Leg en arrière, torso opened to the standing side, one arm back in line with the working leg and the other arm extended forward in front of the torso on the standing-leg side. The forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg. Everyone is agreeing on that now.

The remaining uncertainty is the III/IV pair, and I think the side relationship vs height distinction that Colleague 10 and Colleague 7 raised is the right way to parse it.

Arabesque III is the continuation of that same contralateral opposition, Vaganova’s lower/more closed version of it. The side logic is preserved: the forward arm is still carried on the standing-leg side, opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm staying with the working leg. What changes from II to III is degree of épaulement/croisé, arm height and closeness of the port de bras, not the side relationship. That is why it is taught in the studio as the low opposition arabesque. If you strip out height and inclination, the classic arm-extended-in-front-on-the-opposite-side line remains.

Arabesque IV is where the side relationship actually begins to shift. It is the more pronounced effacé/inclined variation where Vaganova moves the port de bras toward a more en face/ipsilateral presentation and the clear front-back opposition diagonal is softened/lost. In many contemporary syllabi the free arm is brought more over the working-leg side and the clean contralateral front-arm/back-leg line is no longer maintained.

The numbering/translation swap that Colleague 1 flagged explains why the descriptions get mixed up in the literature. Once you hold the side relationship constant and separate it from arm height and épaulement, the two arabesques that retain the defining “arm extended in front on the side contralateral to the lifted leg” port de bras are the two opposition forms in the progression: Arabesque II and Arabesque III.

Arabesque II is unmistakable and there is now essentially consensus. Leg en arrière, torso opened in épaulement to the standing side, port de bras is a straight diagonal: the arm on the working-leg side goes back in line with the leg and the arm on the standing-leg side is taken forward in front of the torso. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

The sticking point is III versus IV, and Colleague 10’s side-relationship vs height distinction is the right way to read it.

Arabesque III is the continuation of that same contralateral opposition in Vaganova, just the lower, more closed version of it. The side logic is preserved: the forward arm is still carried on the standing-leg side, opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm remaining in line with the working leg. What changes from II to III is the lowering/rounding of the arms, a deeper croisé and a more contained port de bras, not the side relationship. If you hold side relationship constant and strip out height and inclination, III retains the classic arm-extended-in-front-on-the-opposite-side line.

Arabesque IV is where Vaganova shifts emphasis. * Arabesque I is the en face/symmetrical arabesque. Arms are essentially in horizontal seconde, palms down, torso essentially square. No single arm is carried in front of the torso in a contralateral diagonal.
* Arabesque III is the closed arabesque. Both arms are brought to the front of the body in a low 1st/2nd front position. The open one-arm-back/one-arm-forward opposition is lost.

The open asymmetrical opposition arabesques are II and IV.

* Arabesque II is the first opposition/croisé arabesque. Leg en arrière, torso opened effacé/croisé to the standing side. Port de bras is a straight diagonal: the arm on the side of the working leg is extended back in line with the leg and the arm on the side of the standing leg is extended forward in front of the torso. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV is the second opposition/effacé arabesque. The same contralateral front-back side relationship is kept as in II: one arm back/up with the working leg and the other arm carried forward in front of the body on the standing-leg side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg. The difference to II is greater torso inclination/effacé and a lower/more closed arm height, not a change of side.

Hence the defining port de bras “an arm extended in front on the side contralateral to the lifted/en arrière leg” is the opposition line of Vaganova Arabesque II and Vaganova Arabesque IV.

The Second-and-Third reading reflects the numbering/translation swap that appears in older pedagogical literature and Cecchetti/French tradition where Russian I/III are rendered differently in English. On the canonical contemporary Vaganova nomenclature taught today the contralateral forward-arm line is II and IV.

B. Second and third

I think we are essentially converged now on Arabesque II, and that’s the anchor for this whole question.

Arabesque I is en face/arms in horizontal seconde, torso essentially square. No contralateral front arm. That is settled.

Arabesque II is the clear first opposition/croisé. Leg en arrière, torso opened to the standing side, one arm back in line with the working leg and the other arm extended forward in front of the torso on the standing-leg side. The forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg. Everyone is agreeing on that now.

The remaining uncertainty is the III/IV pair, and I think the side relationship vs height distinction that Colleague 10 and Colleague 7 raised is the right way to parse it.

Arabesque III is the continuation of that same contralateral opposition, Vaganova’s lower/more closed version of it. The side logic is preserved: the forward arm is still carried on the standing-leg side, opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm staying with the working leg. What changes from II to III is degree of épaulement/croisé, arm height and closeness of the port de bras, not the side relationship. That is why it is taught in the studio as the low opposition arabesque. If you strip out height and inclination, the classic arm-extended-in-front-on-the-opposite-side line remains.

Arabesque IV is where the side relationship actually begins to shift. It is the more pronounced effacé/inclined variation where Vaganova moves the port de bras toward a more en face/ipsilateral presentation and the clear front-back opposition diagonal is softened/lost. In many contemporary syllabi the free arm is brought more over the working-leg side and the clean contralateral front-arm/back-leg line is no longer maintained.

The numbering/translation swap that Colleague 1 flagged explains why the descriptions get mixed up in the literature. Once you hold the side relationship constant and separate it from arm height and épaulement, the two arabesques that retain the defining “arm extended in front on the side contralateral to the lifted leg” port de bras are the two opposition forms in the progression: Arabesque II and Arabesque III.

* Arabesque III is the continuation of the same contralateral opposition as II, just lower/more closed and more croisé. Side logic preserved: forward arm still on standing-leg side opposite lifted leg, back arm with working leg. Height/épaulement change only.
* Arabesque IV is where side relationship shifts toward en face/ipsilateral and the clear front-back opposition diagonal is softened/lost; forward arm moves more toward working-leg side.
Hence contralateral forward arm = II and III.

The numbering/translation swap is repeatedly flagged: older pedagogical literature, Cecchetti/French tradition, and some English summaries interchange Russian I/III and II/IV, leading to descriptions that attach “both arms in front” to III in some sources and “opposition” to III in others. This is the underlying driver of the persistent minority.

Evidence remains definitional/terminological; no authoritative Vaganova syllabus text or primary source has been quoted in the round. Unresolved is exact syllabus wording for Arabesque III port de bras and whether “arm extended in front” is interpreted as a single contralateral arm in opposition vs arms in a general forward plane.

Movement since earlier rounds: strong consolidation toward E. Earlier C First and third positions have collapsed. Persistent minority on III/IV side relationship remains stable at 2 colleagues.

I am tracking both the canonical contemporary numbering I=seconde, II=first opposition, III=closed, IV=second opposition, and the alternative mapping where III retains contralateral opposition and IV shifts ipsilateral. Side relationship for II is agreed; III vs IV side relationship remains the open question.
reflection_text.4:
The question is which Vaganova arabesques en arrière show a port de bras with an arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg, i.e. classic contralateral front-arm / back-leg opposition.

Canonical syllabus description that persists:
* Arabesque I = en face / symmetrical. Arms essentially in horizontal seconde, palms down, torso square or only lightly opened. No single arm carried in front in a contralateral diagonal.
* Arabesque III = closed / both-arms-in-front per majority contemporary teaching. Arms brought low together in front, 1st/2nd front type, open one-back/one-forward opposition lost.
* Arabesque II = first asymmetrical opposition / croisé. Working leg en arrière, torso opened to standing side in épaulement. Port de bras is straight diagonal: arm on working-leg side back with leg, arm on standing-leg side extended forward in front of torso. Forward arm is contralateral to lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = second asymmetrical opposition / effacé. Same contralateral front-back side relationship as II: forward arm on standing-leg side opposite lifted leg, back arm with working leg. Difference from II is greater torso inclination/effacé and lower/more closed arm height, not side relationship.

That gives open opposition arabesques II and IV as the contralateral front-arm forms. This is E. Second and fourth held by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 in round 4, and consistently majority across rounds 0-3. Round 4 tally: E 8, B 2.

Competing view B. Second and third, argued by Colleague 10 and Colleague 7 in round 4. Argument: hold side relationship constant and separate it from arm height/épaulement. Arabesque II is settled contralateral. Arabesque III is claimed as continuation of same contralateral opposition, just lower/more closed with deeper croisé, forward arm still on standing-leg side opposite lifted leg. Arabesque IV is claimed to shift toward more effacé/ipsilateral presentation and soften/lose clear front-back opposition diagonal. Colleague 10 is moving from earlier A. First and second to this B reading; Colleague 7 now separates side relationship from height and claims III preserves contralateral side logic and IV is where side relationship breaks.

Disagreements remain over whether Arabesque III is “both arms in front closed” vs “low opposition continuation” and whether Arabesque IV retains contralateral opposition or shifts ipsilateral. The split is framed as confusion between side relationship vs arm height/épaulement, and a known numbering/translation swap between Vaganova texts and some English/Cecchetti traditions.

Round tallies remain: Round 0: E 5, C 3, A 1, B 1. Round 1: E 8, C 2. Round 2: majority E. Round 3: E 7, B 2. Round 4: E 8, B 2.

Unresolved: nomenclature variation across sources can invert I/II and III/IV numbering, leading to C. First and third claims in earlier rounds. Canonical contemporary Vaganova teaching as described by majority equates contralateral front-arm opposite lifted leg with opposition arabesques II and IV.

Current belief unchanged: E. Second and fourth is best supported under standard Vaganova numbering taught today. The First-and-Third and Second-and-Third views trace to a numbering convention inversion and to conflating arm height/épaulement changes with side relationship changes. Dissent B is strengthening by arguing III is low continuation of opposition and IV is the break point, but majority still defines III as closed both-arms-front and IV as second opposition retaining contralateral side relationship.
